draft.body:
On October 27, 2026, London-based physical AI startup Machenta announced a $40 million seed funding round to develop foundation models that allow robots to learn physical tasks after observing them just once. The investment, co-led by Creandum and Union Square Ventures alongside several angel investors, represents the largest seed funding round raised by a robotics enterprise in the United Kingdom, according to [Imperial College London](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/articles/2026/imperial-ai-spinout-machenta-raises-40-million-to-make-robots-instant-learners/).

Spun out from Imperial College London late last year, Machenta is taking a different direction from the robotics sector's prevailing data-gathering practices. While major robotics developers invest heavily in amassing real-world demonstration data, Machenta develops algorithms that train foundation models completely inside computer-generated simulation environments.

[[FIG1]]

## Simulation Data Replaces Real-World Video Pipelines

Teaching conventional physical AI systems often requires days or weeks of work, relying on hundreds or thousands of human demonstrations to automate a single task. In contrast, Machenta pre-trains its foundation models without using a "single pixel of real-world data," co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Edward Johns told [Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/this-11-person-startup-raised-40-million-train-robots-virtual-worlds-2026-10).

Instead of real-world footage, Machenta generates simulated worlds designed to mimic how objects move and interact. After pre-training on these virtual dynamics, the system can interpret a real-world setting and instruct a robot to execute a task after watching a single human demonstration. Johns likened the workflow to a physical equivalent of vibe coding, as reported by [tech.eu](https://tech.eu/2026/10/27/london-robotics-startup-machenta-raises-40m-seed-investment/).

"Intelligence is not so much about what you can already do, it’s about how quickly you can learn to do something new," Johns said in a statement released by [BusinessCloud](https://businesscloud.co.uk/news/machenta-building-frontier-ai-for-robots-raises-30m/). "Humans don’t need to see the same thing over and over before they can do it. If you take some objects, and show somebody what to do with them, they’ll probably then be able to do the same task immediately."

[[FIG2]]

## Academic Research Background and Technical Limits

The underlying system builds on six years of research at the Imperial College Robot Learning Lab led by Johns, a professor of robot learning in the university's Department of Computing. In early university experiments, researchers guided a robotic arm through a motion manually, such as using a spatula to lift an item. The machine then required roughly 30 minutes of additional environment data collection before it could operate autonomously.

Johns and his former doctoral student Vitalis Vosylius subsequently developed in-context learning algorithms for robotics, adapting techniques that power large language models to physical hardware. Vosylius and Johns founded Machenta to scale the technology, bringing researchers from their Imperial laboratory into the company, according to [Vestbee](https://www.vestbee.com/insights/articles/machenta-lands-40-m). The company has shown that a single underlying model can execute tasks like packaging, assembling, and tidying across multiple platforms, including humanoid hardware.

Machenta has also noted present limits to its technology. Johns told Business Insider that while the model handles tasks like tidying tables and packing boxes, high-precision tasks and complex movements remain difficult challenges.

## Competition in the Physical AI Market

Machenta operates in an increasingly well-funded field featuring heavily capitalized American competitors, as reported by [Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/this-11-person-startup-raised-40-million-train-robots-virtual-worlds-2026-10). California-based developer Physical Intelligence holds a valuation of roughly $11 billion, FieldAI is raising funding at a $10 billion valuation, and Skild AI is valued at more than $14 billion.

Skild AI has already introduced commercial products with single-demonstration features. In August 2026, Skild launched a model designed to carry out previously unseen tasks lasting up to 10 minutes from a single video demonstration. In September 2026, Skild announced it had reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue across more than 60 enterprise clients.

By comparison, Machenta has kept its corporate valuation private and stated it has no immediate plans to commercialize its system, choosing to prioritize foundational research.

## Early Access and Laboratory Expansion

Machenta will use the $40 million seed funding to expand its team and train its model with additional compute and simulated data, while growing operations at its King's Cross office and lab in London, according to [Imperial College London](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/articles/2026/imperial-ai-spinout-machenta-raises-40-million-to-make-robots-instant-learners/).

Although commercial deployment is not scheduled, the startup has opened a waitlist for developers and hardware teams. Through the company's official website at [machenta.com](https://machenta.com/), prospective users can register their target robot hardware and intended manipulation tasks for future access to the model.
